subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 10 periods = 400 minutes
Total: 10 periods · 6h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students discuss their own bus travel experiences and what they noticed along the way (p. 35)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud Rishi's opening journey from Jammu — the bus ride, hairpin roads, Himalayan scenery — while students follow along on Textbook p. 35. The teacher pauses to let the landscape settle in the children's minds.

Students share their own bus or long-distance travel experiences with the class. The teacher prompts: What did you see through the window? What surprised you? What felt different from home? Several children share in turn.

The class discusses what trees and flowers they noticed during a journey (Textbook p. 35). The teacher lists names children offer on the board and asks how the plants changed as the journey moved from one place to another — drawing out the idea that different places have different plants.

Students write two or three sentences in their notebooks: one place they have visited and one plant or tree they noticed there. Those who have not travelled share what they have seen near their home on a walk or trip to the market.

periods.implied_lo: Students can share personal observations from a journey and connect what they saw in one environment to the idea that different places have different plants and landscapes.
periods.section_context: Rishi's bus journey from Jammu through hairpin roads, Himalayan mountain scenery, rose, marigold, hibiscus, tulip, buransh (Rhododendron), children's own travel experiences and plant observations.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask children: 'Did the plants or trees look the same all along your journey, or did they change?' This opens the near-to-far connection the chapter builds on. If many children have not travelled by bus, redirect to any journey — auto, train, or a long walk — so everyone can participate.

periods.activity_title: Road Signs: Match, Read, and Draw
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students draw and label three road signboards not listed in the textbook activity (p. 36)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of road signboards on p. 36

time_bands.activity: The teacher discusses travel safety with the class, drawing on Textbook p. 35 — asking what safety measures children take in a bus, on a bicycle, and while walking on the road. Answers are collected briefly on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 36 and complete the match-the-column activity, pairing signboard images in Column A with their meanings in Column B. The teacher moves around to check understanding and asks children to explain why each sign matters for safety.

Students draw and label any three road signboards they have seen that are not shown in Textbook p. 36. They colour their drawings and write one line about where they saw each sign and what it means. Partners compare their choices.

A quick whole-class share: two or three students hold up their drawings and name their signs. The teacher affirms that signs communicate rules without needing words, connecting to the idea that images carry meaning across language differences.

periods.implied_lo: Students can interpret the meaning of visual symbols in a public space and create original symbols that communicate a safety rule clearly.
periods.section_context: Road signboard match activity, safety measures while travelling, cycling, and walking, student-drawn and labelled road signs.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt children who struggle to recall signs: 'Have you seen a sign near your school gate, the market, or a bus stop?' Encourage them to invent a sign for a hazard they know — this opens up creativity and connects the task to their immediate environment.

periods.activity_title: Flowers of Spring: Observing Regional Plant Diversity
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students find out about mountains, rivers, or streams near where they live and whether they have visited relatives in a far-away place (p. 42)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of tulip, buransh, amaltas, sakhua, and Himalayan landscape

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads the narrative of Rishi arriving at the village and encountering the garden — rose, marigold, hibiscus (familiar to Rishi) and tulip and buransh (new to him). Students look at the textbook illustrations and the teacher asks: Which of these flowers have you seen? Which are new to you?

Students open their notebooks and make a simple two-column observation record: flowers they already knew before today and flowers they learned about in this chapter (tulip, buransh, amaltas, sakhua). For each new flower they write the region it comes from and one thing that makes it special, drawn from the textbook text and illustrations.

Students draw one flower from the new-to-them column and label it with its name, region, and the season it blooms. The teacher circulates and asks: 'Why do you think this flower blooms in spring and not in the cold of winter?'

Brief share: children name one flower they drew and say which region it belongs to. The teacher collects all the regions on the board, helping the class see that the same spring season produces very different flowers across India.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and record plant diversity across regions by naming flowers, their places of origin, and the season in which they bloom.
periods.section_context: Rose, marigold, hibiscus (familiar flowers), tulip (Kashmir), buransh/Rhododendron (Jammu), amaltas/yellow flowers (Kerala-Vishu), sakhua (Jharkhand-Sarhul), Himalayan village garden setting.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why might different mountains and plains have different flowers even in the same season?' Let children guess freely — answers about soil, rain, and cold are all valid and need not be corrected; the goal is noticing diversity, not explaining ecology. If children know local flower names in their own language, encourage them to share.

periods.activity_title: Spring Festivals Across India: A Conversation
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students sing and enjoy the spring song in the textbook (p. 40)

time_bands.activity: The teacher leads the class in singing the spring song on Textbook p. 40 — 'Oh! Spring is in the air…' — once together, then a second time with students clapping along. The tone is joyful and unhurried. The teacher then asks: What does spring feel like, sound like, look like?

The teacher narrates the three spring festivals from the chapter — Kashmir Tulip Festival, Jammu's spring ritual (mustard and buransh at doorsteps, elders' blessings), Kerala's Vishu (Vishu Kani with amaltas flowers) — and the Sarhul festival of Jharkhand from the 'Do You Know' box, where people process to the sakhua tree with germinated grains and sakhua flowers, singing with dhol and nagada. After each festival, the teacher pauses and asks: Is there something similar in your family or place?

Students discuss: How do festivals bring communities together? The teacher guides the conversation toward the idea that flowers, food, music, and gathering are common threads, even as the specific plants, rituals, and names differ across regions.

Students write one sentence: 'One spring festival I know is ___, and people celebrate it by ___.' Those whose family celebrates a different season's festival write that one — the goal is connecting personal experience to the chapter's idea of nature and celebration.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect regional festival practices to the season they celebrate, identifying common threads — flowers, community gathering, food, music — across different cultural traditions.
periods.section_context: Spring song (Textbook p. 40), Kashmir Tulip Festival, Jammu spring ritual with mustard and buransh flowers, Kerala Vishu and Vishu Kani with amaltas, Jharkhand Sarhul with sakhua tree and sakhua flowers, germinated grains, dhol and nagada.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Mami says spring is a celebration of nature — what does she mean?' Encourage children to link the specific flower of each region to what people do with it during the festival. If children mention a festival not in the textbook, welcome it warmly — the chapter's spirit is that there are many more celebrations than it can name.

periods.activity_title: Seasons and Festivals: An Elder-Inquiry Write Task
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students ask elders about festivals celebrated in their locality for each season and list special foods prepared during these festivals (p. 40)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 40 and shows the four-season festival table. Together the class reads the instructions: for each season, find the name of a festival celebrated in their own locality and the special food prepared. The teacher models one example from a well-known festival to show how the table works.

Students attempt to fill in as much of the table as they can from their own knowledge — what they have seen at home, heard from family, or experienced themselves. The teacher circulates and prompts: 'What do people cook at your home during that time of year? What does your grandmother prepare?'

Students share what they have written with a partner, comparing which festivals and foods match and which differ. The teacher then leads a brief whole-class share where two or three different festivals per season are collected on the board, showing regional variety.

Students write a homework inquiry prompt in their notebooks: 'Tonight I will ask an elder in my family: What festivals do we celebrate in each season, and what special food do we make?' They will bring the answer to share. The teacher also asks students to write one thing they are curious to find out.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple inquiry by asking an elder a structured question about seasonal festivals and foods, and record the response as organised information.
periods.section_context: Four-season festival and food table (Textbook p. 40), elder-inquiry task, locally known festival names, special festival foods named by students.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Do you think the same festival is celebrated the same way everywhere in India, or does it change from place to place?' This primes children for the diversity they will find when they ask elders. Accept all answers — the inquiry itself matters more than getting a 'correct' festival name.

periods.activity_title: Festival Foods and Clothes: Matching and Writing
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students match festival foods to their festivals from the given list (p. 41)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook illustrations of festival foods on p. 41

time_bands.activity: Students open Textbook p. 41 and look at the food-festival match activity. The teacher reads aloud each food name — thekua, pitha, plum cake, gujiya, sadya, holige, seviyan — and asks: Has anyone tasted any of these? Students briefly share.

Students complete the match activity — pairing each food with its festival: Thekua–Chhath Puja, Pitha–Bihu, Plum Cake–Christmas, Gujiya–Holi, Sadya–Onam, Holige–Ugadi, Seviyan–Eid-ul-Fitr. The teacher circulates, asking children to say which part of India each festival is associated with.

Students respond in writing to the question on Textbook p. 41: What special dresses do you wear during festivals? They write three to four sentences describing their own festival clothing — colours, style, when it is worn — and may draw a small sketch alongside if they wish.

A class share of two or three responses to the dress question. The teacher draws out the observation that clothes, like foods, vary by region, community, and festival — and asks: 'Is there one festival dress everyone wears, or many different ones?' This connects to the chapter's diversity theme.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe cultural diversity by matching festival-specific foods to their festivals and describing their own festival clothing practices.
periods.section_context: Thekua (Chhath Puja), pitha (Bihu), plum cake (Christmas), gujiya (Holi), sadya (Onam), holige (Ugadi), seviyan (Eid-ul-Fitr), festival dress descriptions from students.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: After the match activity, ask: 'Why do you think Onam has sadya — a meal of many dishes served on a banana leaf — while Christmas has plum cake? What might the land or season have to do with it?' This draws out the nature-culture link. Accept children's own food names if they know a regional variant.

periods.activity_title: Do All Families Celebrate the Same Way? Reflecting on Inclusion
periods.textbook_anchor: Festival of Flowers — Students find out whether everyone celebrates festivals with a variety of special food and new clothes (p. 42)

time_bands.activity: The teacher reads aloud the 'Find out' task on Textbook p. 42: 'Do you think everyone celebrates festivals with a variety of special food and new clothes?' The teacher asks children to think silently for a moment before anyone answers. The question is posed openly — no right answer is given yet.

Students discuss in pairs: Do all families in their neighbourhood celebrate the same way? Do all children get new clothes and special food at every festival? The teacher then opens to the whole group and collects responses on the board without judgment, noting both 'yes' and 'no' answers and the reasons children give.

The teacher guides the class toward the value the chapter implies: that festivals are for joy and togetherness, and that people celebrate in different ways depending on what they have. Children discuss: How can we make sure everyone feels included during a festival? What could they do at school or at home?

Students write one or two sentences in their notebooks: 'One way I can include others during a festival is ___.' The teacher reads a few responses aloud and affirms the class's thinking before closing.

periods.implied_lo: Students can examine a social pattern — who participates in festival celebrations and how — and articulate a concrete action that promotes inclusion during celebrations.
periods.section_context: Find-out task about whether everyone celebrates with special food and new clothes (Textbook p. 42), student-identified ways to include others during festivals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Have you ever seen a friend who did not join in a celebration? How do you think that felt?' Let the conversation be sensitive and unhurried — children may share real experiences. Affirm that noticing is the first step, and that small acts of sharing and invitation matter.

periods.activity_title: Let Us Reflect: Discussing Travel, Safety, and Nature
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss modes of transport, travel safety, special festival foods, how festivals bring people together, and joy in nature (p. 42)

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 42 and introduces the 'Let us reflect' section. Students read the five discussion prompts together. The teacher explains that this is a chance to revisit the whole chapter's big ideas through conversation.

The class discusses each prompt in turn: modes of transport used during travel; how one can be safe during travels; special foods prepared during festivals; how festivals and celebrations bring people together; and whether spending time in nature brings joy. The teacher encourages children to draw on the chapter's narrative — Rishi's journey, the village festivals, the mountain flowers — as well as their own experiences.

Students respond to the two 'Write' tasks on Textbook p. 42: naming two relatives they have visited recently, and writing how they spend time with cousins and relatives. Two or three students share their responses.

Students complete the fill-in-the-blanks on Textbook p. 42 — mountains, hairpin roads, mud road, buransh, haakh — in their notebooks. The teacher checks answers together as a class, reading each completed sentence aloud.

periods.implied_lo: Students can revisit and articulate the chapter's key ideas — transport, travel safety, festival foods, community, and nature — by connecting them to their own lived experiences.
periods.section_context: Five discussion prompts (modes of transport, travel safety, festival foods, festivals and community, joy in nature), two write tasks (relatives visited, time with cousins), fill-in-the-blanks (mountains, hairpin roads, mud road, buransh, haakh).
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: For the discussion prompt 'Do you feel happy spending time in nature?', let children describe specific places — a garden, a field, a river bank, a rooftop — rather than answering in the abstract. This keeps the conversation grounded and personal, consistent with the chapter's near-to-far approach.

periods.activity_title: Design Your Own Signboard: Creative Expression
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students draw signboards for school spaces on chart paper using images and colours of their choice, then explain what they created (p. 43)
materials: Chart paper (one half-sheet per student or pair)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook p. 43 task showing the list of seven school spaces

time_bands.activity: The teacher opens Textbook p. 43 and reads the signboard task. The seven spaces are listed on the board: School library, Toilet, Assembly, Drinking water point, Playground, My classroom, Stairs. The teacher asks: What image would YOU use for each of these? Why? A few quick ideas are shared.

Students (working individually or in pairs) choose any four of the seven spaces and design signboards on their chart paper — selecting their own image and colour, and writing the space's name as a label. The teacher circulates and asks: 'Will someone who cannot read the label understand your sign? What makes a sign clear?'

Students share their signboards with the class by holding them up and explaining what they designed and why they chose that image. Two or three students per space (where multiple children chose the same space) compare their designs. The class notices how different images can communicate the same message.

Brief close: the teacher draws the connection to road signboards seen earlier in the chapter — signs work across language because images carry meaning. Students are invited to notice signboards in their school and neighbourhood with fresh eyes.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design a visual symbol that communicates a specific meaning clearly, and explain the reasoning behind their design choices.
periods.section_context: Creative signboard design task for seven school spaces (School library, Toilet, Assembly, Drinking water point, Playground, My classroom, Stairs), student explanations of design choices, connection to road signboards.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If someone from another country visited our school and could not read our language, would your signboard still work for them?' This extends the task toward the idea that visual communication crosses language — a concrete and satisfying discovery for Grade III children.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Students discuss how festivals and celebrations bring people together (p. 42)

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a large web on the board with 'Spring' at the centre and arms extending outward. The class collectively recalls all the spring festivals from the chapter — Kashmir Tulip Festival, Jammu spring ritual with buransh and mustard, Vishu with amaltas in Kerala, Sarhul with sakhua in Jharkhand — and the flowers, foods, and rituals linked to each. The teacher fills the web with the class's contributions.

The teacher poses the synthesis question: 'The chapter shows us four very different festivals — different plants, different rituals, different foods. What do they all have in common?' Students discuss in groups of three or four, then share. The teacher guides the class toward: spring arrives, nature renews itself, and people across India celebrate that renewal — each in their own way.

Each student draws a 'festival moment' of their own choosing — it may be one of the chapter's four festivals or a festival from their own life — showing a flower, a food, and a community action (a gathering, a ritual, a sharing). They write one sentence underneath: 'This is ___ celebrated in ___, where people ___.' The drawing and sentence are their own synthesis of the chapter's dual theme: nature changes, and people celebrate together.

A gallery share: students hold up or lay down their drawings and walk past each other's work. The teacher closes by naming what the class has built together — the understanding that across India's many landscapes and communities, the joy of spring and the habit of celebration connect people to nature and to one another.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise the chapter's central idea — that seasonal change in nature is marked by cultural celebration — by connecting specific regional examples of flowers, foods, and festivals to the shared human impulse to celebrate renewal.
periods.section_context: Whole-chapter synthesis: Kashmir Tulip Festival, Jammu spring ritual (buransh, mustard flowers, elders' blessings), Kerala Vishu (amaltas, Vishu Kani), Jharkhand Sarhul (sakhua tree, sakhua flowers, germinated grains, dhol, nagada), spring song, festival foods (thekua, pitha, gujiya, sadya, holige, seviyan, plum cake), festival clothing, road signboards, travel safety, Rishi's journey through the Himalayas.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Is there a festival near you where people go outside into nature — to a garden, a river, a tree, or a field — as part of the celebration?' This draws out the sakhua procession, Vishu Kani at dawn, and the tulip garden as common threads, and invites children's own knowledge of nature-linked celebrations into the synthesis.

assessment_items.question_text: Rishi travelled from Jammu to a mountain village. Along the way, he saw flowers he had never seen before. Which flower did he see for the first time in the mountain village?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. Rose, marigold, and hibiscus are stated in the chapter as flowers Rishi already recognised — they were familiar to him. Only buransh and tulip were new. If a student selects buransh, they have read carefully; if they select rose, marigold, or hibiscus, they have confused familiar with new.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can share personal observations from a journey and connect what they saw in one environment to the idea that different places have different plants and landscapes.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing Rose indicates the student did not distinguish between Rishi's familiar flowers and the new ones he encountered — rose is explicitly a flower he already knew.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing Marigold shows the same confusion — marigold is among the flowers Rishi recognised from home, not a new discovery.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing Hibiscus reflects the same engagement failure — hibiscus is listed alongside rose and marigold as a familiar flower for Rishi, not a new one from the Himalayan village.

assessment_items.question_text: A road sign shows a picture of a child walking inside a triangle with a red border. What does this sign most likely mean, and why would it be placed near a school?
expected_elements: Identifies the sign as a warning or caution sign for drivers
States that the sign means children may be crossing the road or that this is a school zone
Explains that it is placed near a school so drivers slow down and are careful because children walk there
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any response that correctly identifies the sign as a warning to drivers about the presence of children, even if the student uses different words. Award full credit for all three elements; partial credit for two. The explanation of placement is the key reasoning step.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret the meaning of visual symbols in a public space and create original symbols that communicate a safety rule clearly.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

expected_elements: Identifies the sign as a warning or caution sign for drivers
States that the sign means children may be crossing the road or that this is a school zone
Explains that it is placed near a school so drivers slow down and are careful because children walk there

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes four flowers that bloom in spring in different parts of India. Which flower is associated with the Sarhul festival celebrated in Jharkhand?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is D. Sakhua is explicitly named in the 'Do You Know' box as the tree and flower central to the Sarhul festival of Jharkhand. Tulip is linked to the Kashmir Tulip Festival; amaltas is linked to Kerala's Vishu; buransh is linked to Jammu's spring ritual. Confusion among these four is the primary expected error.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and record plant diversity across regions by naming flowers, their places of origin, and the season in which they bloom.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes diversity among plants, and birds and animals in their immediate environment (shape, sounds, food habits, growth, habitat)

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing Tulip indicates the student has confused the Sarhul festival with the Kashmir Tulip Festival — a region-flower mix-up within the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing Amaltas shows the student has confused Jharkhand's Sarhul with Kerala's Vishu, which features the amaltas/yellow flower.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing Buransh reflects a confusion between Jharkhand and Jammu — buransh is the flower of Jammu's spring ritual, not Sarhul.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, Mami says: 'Spring is a celebration of nature.' Rishi learns about four different spring festivals — in Kashmir, Jammu, Kerala, and Jharkhand. Choose any two of these festivals and explain: What flower is important in that festival, and what do people do with it or during it? Then explain what you think Mami means.
look_for: Names two spring festivals correctly and identifies the specific flower associated with each

Describes at least one cultural action or ritual associated with each named festival (e.g., Vishu Kani ritual with amaltas, procession to sakhua tree in Sarhul, buransh at doorsteps with elders' blessings, tulip garden visits in Kashmir)
Attempts to explain Mami's statement by connecting the flower-blooming of spring to the human act of celebration — showing that nature's renewal is what people are marking
Uses chapter vocabulary (at least two of: tulip, buransh, amaltas, sakhua, Vishu Kani, Sarhul, spring) in a meaningful way
assessment_items.annotation: A strong response names two festivals correctly, links the right flower to each, describes a ritual action, and offers a genuine attempt to interpret Mami's statement as connecting nature's change to human celebration. A weak response names festivals without linking them to flowers or actions, or copies the statement without explaining it. Award partial credit for one festival described well.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect regional festival practices to the season they celebrate, identifying common threads — flowers, community gathering, food, music — across different cultural traditions.

assessment_items.question_text: Anjali wants to find out which festivals are celebrated in her locality during summer and what special foods are made. She decides to ask her grandmother. Write two questions Anjali could ask her grandmother to find out this information.
expected_elements: Includes at least one question that asks about the name of a summer festival celebrated locally
Includes at least one question that asks about a specific food prepared during that festival
Questions are phrased clearly enough that an elder could understand and answer them
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two clearly phrased questions that address festival names and festival foods. The specific festival or food named is not the criterion — the ability to frame an inquiry question is. Regional variation in festival names and foods is expected and all answers are acceptable. Award full credit for two functional questions covering both elements; partial credit for one good question.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple inquiry by asking an elder a structured question about seasonal festivals and foods, and record the response as organised information.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

Includes at least one question that asks about a specific food prepared during that festival

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter shows that different festivals across India have their own special foods. Which food is matched correctly with its festival?
assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is C. Seviyan–Eid-ul-Fitr is one of the seven correct pairings from the textbook match activity. Gujiya belongs to Holi (not Onam); Sadya belongs to Onam (not Holi); Pitha belongs to Bihu (not Christmas). Each distractor swaps a food with a plausible but incorrect festival from within the same chapter activity.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe and describe cultural diversity by matching festival-specific foods to their festivals and describing their own festival clothing practices.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing Gujiya–Onam shows the student has confused Gujiya's festival (Holi) with Onam — two festivals from the same match list, both involving celebration but from different regions and seasons.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing Sadya–Holi shows a swap between Onam's food (sadya) and Holi's festival — the student may have remembered the food name but not its correct pairing.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing Pitha–Christmas shows confusion between Bihu (the correct festival for pitha, an Assamese rice cake) and Christmas — possibly because both involve special baked or sweet preparations.

assessment_items.task: Think about a festival you know. Do all families in your neighbourhood celebrate this festival the same way — with the same food, new clothes, and decorations? Draw a picture of how your family celebrates and write two sentences: one about what your family does, and one about how you could make the celebration more welcoming for a friend who celebrates differently.
assessment_items.scaffold: My family celebrates ___ by ___. One way I could include a friend who celebrates differently is ___.
format_of_output: A drawing of a festival moment
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any festival the student chooses — responses will vary by region, religion, and family practice, and all are valid. The key assessment element is the second sentence: does the student articulate a genuine, concrete inclusive action (sharing food, inviting a friend, explaining a tradition) rather than a vague or generic statement? Regional variation in festival practices is expected and celebrated here.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can examine a social pattern — who participates in festival celebrations and how — and articulate a concrete action that promotes inclusion during celebrations.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can observe a social pattern in festival participation, recognise that not all families celebrate equally, and think of a concrete inclusive action — showing both awareness and a values-based response.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The first sentence describes the student's own family practice. The second sentence — the more important one — asks for an action word: invite, share, explain, include. A strong response names something specific (share my family's sweet with a neighbour, invite a friend to watch our ritual), not just 'be kind'.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific festival, describes a concrete family practice, and offers a specific inclusive action. Weak: names a festival but leaves the second sentence as 'I will be nice to everyone' or leaves it blank.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who do not celebrate any festival may write about a community gathering, a neighbourhood event, or a seasonal occasion they know. Students with limited writing ability may dictate their sentences to the teacher or submit the drawing alone with an oral explanation.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing externalises the festival scene concretely, supporting Grade III students who express themselves more easily through images. The scaffold ensures both a personal description and a values reflection are present.

assessment_items.question_text: In the chapter, the children discuss how people travel to visit relatives. Which of the following is the best example of staying safe while travelling on a road?

options.label: A
options.text: Crossing the road quickly wherever you like

options.label: B
options.text: Playing on the pavement near a busy road

options.label: C
options.text: Riding a bicycle without looking at the road signs

options.label: D
options.text: Walking on the side of the road facing the traffic

assessment_items.annotation: The correct answer is A. Walking on the side of the road facing traffic is a travel safety rule discussed in the chapter's safety tasks. The three distractors each represent a specific unsafe behaviour covered or implied in the chapter's discussion of road safety: crossing anywhere (jaywalking), playing near traffic, and ignoring road signs.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can revisit and articulate the chapter's key ideas — transport, travel safety, festival foods, community, and nature — by connecting them to their own lived experiences.

competency.competency_text: Asks questions and makes predictions about simple patterns (season change, food chain, phases of the moon, movement of stars and planets, shapes of trees, plants, leaves, and flowers, rituals, celebrations) observed in the immediate environment

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'Crossing the road quickly wherever you like' shows the student has not connected the road safety discussion to the rule about using crossings and zebra lines — they may know that speed is sometimes important but have not applied it to pedestrian safety.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'Playing on the pavement near a busy road' shows the student has not recognised that proximity to traffic is itself a hazard — they may think the pavement is always safe regardless of activity.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing 'Riding a bicycle without looking at road signs' shows the student has engaged with bicycles in the chapter but has not connected sign-reading to safety — reversing the purpose of road signs.

assessment_items.task: Design a signboard for one of these school spaces: the school library, the drinking water point, or the playground. Use any image and colour you like. When you are done, write one sentence explaining what your sign means and why someone who cannot read the words would still understand it.
assessment_items.scaffold: My sign shows ___ because ___. Even without reading the words, a person would know this is ___ because ___.
format_of_output: A drawn and coloured signboard with a label
Two sentences following the scaffold explaining the design and its clarity
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any image the student chooses for the sign — there is no single correct design. Assess whether the drawn image clearly communicates the intended space (a book for library, a water tap for drinking water, a ball or swing for playground) and whether the student's explanation shows awareness that the image should communicate without words.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design a visual symbol that communicates a specific meaning clearly, and explain the reasoning behind their design choices.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can select and draw a visual image that communicates a specific meaning, and can articulate why the image works as a symbol — showing the beginning of design thinking and visual communication awareness.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The first sentence names the image chosen and the reasoning. The second sentence — more important — asks the student to think from the viewer's perspective: would someone unfamiliar with the words still understand the sign? Strong responses name a specific feature of the drawing that makes it clear (a water drop shape, a book outline, a swing).
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: draws a recognisable image clearly linked to the space, labels it, and explains why the image alone would communicate. Weak: draws an image with no clear link to the space, or writes only that 'it looks nice' without explaining the communicative logic.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students with fine-motor challenges may use simple geometric shapes or a combination of colours and a single icon. Students who complete the design quickly may add a second sign for a different space. Oral explanation is accepted in place of written sentences.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The drawing is the primary product — it externalises the student's design thinking. The scaffold sentences require the student to move from making to explaining, which is the higher-order step this task is assessing.

assessment_items.question_text: The chapter shows that across India, people celebrate the arrival of spring through different festivals — the Kashmir Tulip Festival, Jammu's spring ritual, Kerala's Vishu, and Jharkhand's Sarhul. Each festival uses a different flower and has its own special rituals and foods. What do all these festivals have in common? Use examples from the chapter to explain your answer.
look_for: Identifies at least two shared features across the spring festivals (e.g., all involve a flower that blooms in spring; all bring communities together; all involve some form of special food, ritual, or celebration of nature's renewal)
Uses specific examples from the chapter to support at least one shared feature — naming at least two festivals by name and linking each to a flower, food, or ritual
Articulates the idea that even though the specific practices differ by region, the underlying impulse — celebrating spring and nature's renewal — is shared
Attempts to connect the natural change (flowers blooming, grass growing, new leaves) to the human response (celebration, gathering, ritual)
assessment_items.annotation: This is a synthesis item drawing the entire chapter's dual strand together. A strong response names multiple festivals, identifies a genuine common thread, and shows the student has understood that nature's seasonal change drives human celebration. A weak response lists festival names without connecting them or copies a phrase from the chapter without explanation. Award partial credit for responses that identify one common feature well with one good example.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise the chapter's central idea — that seasonal change in nature is marked by cultural celebration — by connecting specific regional examples of flowers, foods, and festivals to the shared human impulse to celebrate renewal.
